## Three risk conversations, one new system

The eQMS (electronic quality-management system) project has a name, a budget line, and — as of
this week's planning meeting — a go-live target. It's the system Lakeshore has needed for a
while: one place to hold CAPA (corrective and preventive action) records, document control, and
internal-audit logs across all three sites, replacing a patchwork of spreadsheets, a BECS-adjacent
tool nobody loves, and — at Fairview specifically — a fair amount of paper that `fda-and-aabb-in-
practice` already put on the record. You're not here to fix Fairview's paper problem today; the
eQMS is simply the reason it keeps coming up.

Your Quality Analyst opens with a risk question, and she opens it well: "Before we migrate CAPA
records into this thing, I want to run a proper risk assessment on the cutover — what could go
wrong, how bad, how we'd catch it." She's already reaching for Risk Identification, Risk Analysis,
likelihood and severity and detectability scores — the ICH Q9(R1) vocabulary `quality-risk-
management` built into her. It's rigorous, it's documented, and it's going to produce exactly the
kind of artifact an assessor would want to see.

Your systems administrator has a risk question too, about the same system: who gets administrative
access to the new eQMS, how that access is provisioned and reviewed, what happens if the migration
window gets interrupted partway through. He's not wrong to worry about any of it. But watch how he
says it: "I'll just make sure the usual people have the usual access, and we'll keep an eye on it
after launch." No named process, no written threshold, no document that will exist six months from
now when someone asks why access was granted the way it was. It's a real risk judgment — he's been
doing this job long enough to make good calls — it just never gets built into anything.

Two competent people, one new system, two completely different risk conversations, and no shared
place where either conversation shows up next to the other. That gap is this module's whole
subject. The eQMS is the first system at Lakeshore that genuinely needs both: real quality risk
thinking, because its records feed AABB and FDA-facing decisions, and real security/operational
risk thinking, because it's new infrastructure spanning three sites with nothing today playing the
IT-security-flavored role your QA's ICH Q9 work already plays for quality. You're about to go
looking for a third framework — not to replace what your QA already runs well, but to give the
eQMS one framework that runs start to finish, instead of two that never talk to each other.

No citations yet. Just a planning meeting, two risk conversations running in parallel, and the
honest realization that "we've always handled this informally" was fine when the stakes were
smaller than a three-site system of record.

## Why this matters — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure this module is actually about preventing, and it's not "the eQMS gets hacked"
or "the eQMS loses a CAPA record" in isolation — plenty of individual controls can prevent either
of those. The failure is subtler and more corrosive: **a system goes live with risk reasoning that
exists, is probably even correct, and is scattered across people's heads and a handful of
disconnected documents in two different vocabularies** — so that six months later, when something
goes wrong, nobody can reconstruct *why* a given risk was judged acceptable, who signed off on
that judgment, or whether anyone ever checked that the controls built to address it actually work.
Your QA's ICH Q9 process would survive that question for the quality side. Nothing survives it for
the security side, because nothing is written down.

You already know this shape of problem from ITSM, just under different names. Think about the
difference between an organization that runs a real **Service Design** and **Service Transition**
practice for every new service — sizing it, picking controls, testing them, getting a documented
go-live decision, then monitoring it in **Continual Improvement** — versus one where every team
ad-libs its own launch checklist. Both might ship something that works. Only one can answer an
auditor's "why" six months later, and only one catches the slow-drifting problem a one-time
checklist was never built to catch. RMF (Risk Management Framework), ISO 31000, and ICH Q9 are
three different industries' answers to "what does real Service Transition for *risk decisions*
look like," written by three very different kinds of body. Lakeshore already runs one of them
well. This module looks at the other two, not to replace what works, but to find a structure that
can finally hold the systems administrator's half of the conversation — and apply it to the eQMS,
end to end, across this course's next four modules.

One honest note before you go further, the same one `the-aabb-assessment-process` already taught
you to make about AABB accreditation: **borrowing a framework's structure is not the same as being
legally bound by it.** Lakeshore volunteered into AABB accreditation because Riverside General and
other hospital customers expect it, not because federal law requires it. What you're about to do
with RMF is the identical move, aimed at a different gap: adopt a structure voluntarily because it
names a motion worth running consistently, not because anyone is required to run it.

## The same motion, three vocabularies

Strip away each framework's own words and all three are doing the same six things, in roughly the
same order, for every risk decision they govern:

1. **Identify and assess the risk** — name what could go wrong and how bad it would be.
2. **Decide how to respond** — reduce it, accept it, or some mix of both.
3. **Implement that response** — actually build the control, process, or safeguard.
4. **Verify the response works** — check, ideally independently, that the control does what it's
   supposed to.
5. **Accept the residual risk**, formally or informally — someone with standing says "what's left
   is tolerable" on the record.
6. **Keep monitoring** — because a risk judgment made once, at launch, goes stale.

Here's how each framework names that same motion:

**NIST's Risk Management Framework (RMF)** — from NIST (the National Institute of Standards and
Technology, a U.S. federal agency) — names it as **seven sequential steps**: Prepare, Categorize,
Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor. RMF is documented in NIST Special Publication
(SP) 800-37, Revision 2 (the current version, finalized December 2018). Two things worth being
precise about before you borrow it. First: **Prepare is Revision 2's own addition** — earlier
versions of RMF, and most older public material describing it, show a six-step cycle without it.
This course works from the current, seven-step version, and says so honestly rather than quietly
treating Prepare as if it had always been there. Second, and more important: **RMF is written for
U.S. federal information systems.** Its own text says it's carried out by "a senior Federal
official" on behalf of an agency. Lakeshore is a private blood establishment. Nothing in federal
law requires Lakeshore to run RMF, issue anything resembling a federal authorization, or use any
of SP 800-37's vocabulary at all. What you're about to do — the same thing this curriculum has
already shown Lakeshore doing with ICH Q9's structure and AABB's own accreditation structure — is
**borrow RMF's structure voluntarily** because it names the categorize→select→implement→assess→
authorize→monitor motion with unusual precision, not because anyone outranks Lakeshore into using
it.

**ISO 31000**, "Risk management — Guidelines," is published by ISO (the International Organization
for Standardization) — an international standards body, not a government agency and not an
industry-specific regulator. It's deliberately generic: usable by any organization, for any kind
of risk, in any sector. ISO 31000 is a paid standard; this curriculum has never independently
purchased, fetched, or quoted its actual text — the same handling already given to AABB Standards,
GAMP 5, and ISO 19011 elsewhere. What can be said honestly, in this course's own words, is the
general shape of the risk-management *process* ISO 31000 is publicly known to describe: establishing
the context a risk decision sits in, assessing the risk (identifying, analyzing, and evaluating
it), treating the risk (choosing and applying a response), monitoring and reviewing it over time,
and recording and reporting the whole decision. That's five recurring activities this course will
refer to — described from the outside, not quoted, and not asserted as an exact, complete,
word-for-word enumeration of the standard's own structure, since nobody on this project has read
the paid document itself.

**ICH Q9(R1)**, already taught in full in `quality-system-essentials`'s `quality-risk-management`
module, names the same motion as **four stages**: Risk Assessment (itself broken into
Identification, Analysis, and Evaluation), Risk Control (Reduction and Acceptance), Risk
Communication, and Risk Review. ICH (the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical
Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use) is a harmonized international guideline body for
pharmaceuticals and biologics specifically — guidance-tier, not a government regulation, but
adopted by regulators including FDA as the accepted method for defensible quality risk assessment
in this industry. Your QA already runs this one fluently; this module names it only to put it next
to the other two, not to re-derive its stages or re-run its FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects
Analysis) example.

Lined up against the six-step motion, the honest mapping looks like this — and it's genuinely
uneven, not a clean one-to-one swap of vocabulary:

| The underlying motion | NIST RMF | ISO 31000 (described, not quoted) | ICH Q9(R1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Get ready to make the call | **Prepare** | *(folded into establishing context)* | *(no distinct stage — assumed before Risk Assessment begins)* |
| Identify and assess the risk | **Categorize** | Establishing context, then risk assessment | **Risk Assessment** (Identification/Analysis/Evaluation) |
| Decide and build the response | **Select**, then **Implement** | Risk treatment | **Risk Control** — Reduction half |
| Verify the response works | **Assess** | *(folded into monitoring and review)* | *(implicit — verification feeds Risk Review)* |
| Accept the residual risk, on the record | **Authorize** | *(no single named decision point)* | **Risk Control** — Acceptance half |
| Share the decision with the people who need it | *(threaded through RMF's tasks, no separate step)* | Recording and reporting | **Risk Communication** |
| Keep watching | **Monitor** | Monitoring and review | **Risk Review** |

Notice what that table actually shows, because it's the real point of this module, not a footnote
to it: **the genuine differences aren't just vocabulary.** RMF is the only one of the three with a
single, named, formal decision point — Authorize — where one accountable person looks at the whole
picture and says, on the record, "this risk is acceptable, operate." ISO 31000, true to being a
general-purpose standard usable for any risk in any organization, never names one universal
sign-off gate the way RMF does; risk treatment and acceptance happen, but ISO 31000 doesn't force
them through a single named ceremony. ICH Q9(R1) comes closest to RMF's shape — Risk Acceptance is
a real, deliberate decision Q9 insists on — but it's scoped to pharmaceutical and biologics quality
risk specifically, and this curriculum has already built it out in real depth. RMF is also the
only one of the three written for a specific *kind* of organization (U.S. federal agencies) rather
than a specific *kind* of risk (ISO 31000) or a specific *industry* (ICH Q9). That's exactly why
RMF's structure is the one worth borrowing for the eQMS: it's the only one of the three built
around a system going live, with a named, accountable, yes/no moment attached to it — which is
precisely the gap your systems administrator's informal "I'll keep an eye on it" left open.

## Citation decoder

NIST Special Publications use a different citation shape than anything else in this curriculum so
far: a document number and revision (`SP 800-37 Rev. 2`), then a chapter and section number
(`3.2`) instead of a CFR-style part/section/paragraph. Read `SP 800-37 Rev. 2, §3.2` aloud as
"Special Publication eight-hundred-thirty-seven, Revision two, section three point two" — the same
way you'd read any numbered technical document.

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Ch. 2 (Figure 2 framing) | "Special Publication eight-hundred-thirty-seven, Revision two, Chapter Two" | U.S. government work, public domain, safe to quote verbatim. Describes, in sequence, what the Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, and Monitor steps each do. | The five-step backbone of what modules 2 through 5 will actually build for the eQMS. |
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, §3.1 (Prepare's purpose) | "...section three point one" | Same tier. States why Prepare exists as its own step. | The honest answer to "why does RMF have seven steps now instead of six." |
| NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, §3.2 (Categorize's purpose) | "...section three point two" | Same tier. States what the Categorize step is actually deciding. | What module 2 will apply directly to the eQMS's CAPA, document-control, and audit-log data. |
| ICH Q9(R1) | "The ICH Q9, Revision 1, Quality Risk Management guideline" | Guideline-tier, reused from `quality-risk-management` — a harmonized method, not a numbered legal requirement. Not re-quoted here. | The third point of comparison — already fully built, named only. |
| ISO 31000 | "ISO three-one-thousand" | A paid international standard — named and described in this course's own words only, never quoted. No part/section citation exists in this curriculum because the text itself hasn't been read. | The second point of comparison — general-purpose, industry-agnostic, no authorization-style gate. |

## The actual text

Figure 2's own framing of what five of the seven steps do, from NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Chapter Two
(page 9) — U.S. government work, public domain, quoted verbatim from `sources/nist/sp-800-37r2-
excerpt.md`:

> Select an initial set of controls for the system and tailor the controls as needed to reduce
> risk to an acceptable level based on an assessment of risk.
> Implement the controls and describe how the controls are employed within the system and
> its environment of operation.
> Assess the controls to determine if the controls are implemented correctly, operating as
> intended, and producing the desired outcomes with respect to satisfying the security and
> privacy requirements.
> Authorize the system or common controls based on a determination that the risk to
> organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation is
> acceptable.
> Monitor the system and the associated controls on an ongoing basis to include assessing
> control effectiveness, documenting changes to the system and environment of operation,
> conducting risk assessments and impact analyses, and reporting the security and privacy
> posture of the system.

Read that against ISO 31000's five themes and ICH Q9's four stages above: "Select... tailor the
controls... to reduce risk to an acceptable level" is risk treatment, is Risk Control. "Assess the
controls to determine if [they are]... producing the desired outcomes" is verification, is the
half of Risk Review that actually checks a control works. "Authorize... based on a determination
that the risk... is acceptable" is the one moment none of the other two frameworks names quite as
sharply — a single, dated, accountable decision.

On sequencing, immediately following that passage, quoted verbatim:

> While the RMF steps are listed in sequential order above and in Chapter Three, the steps
> following the Prepare step can be carried out in a nonsequential order.

Worth sitting with that line, because it undercuts the tidiest possible misreading of this whole
module: none of these three frameworks is actually a straight line you walk once and file away.
ISO 31000's monitoring-and-review theme and ICH Q9's Risk Review stage both say the same thing in
their own words — these are cycles, not checklists.

The Prepare step's own purpose statement, quoted verbatim:

> The purpose of the Prepare step is to carry out essential activities at the organization,
> mission and business process, and information system levels of the organization to
> help prepare the organization to manage its security and privacy risks using the Risk
> Management Framework.

And the Categorize step's own purpose statement — the one module 2 will actually apply to the
eQMS — quoted verbatim:

> The purpose of the Categorize step is to inform organizational risk management processes and
> tasks by determining the adverse impact to organizational operations and assets, individuals,
> other organizations, and the Nation with respect to the loss of confidentiality, integrity, and
> availability of organizational systems and the information processed, stored, and transmitted by
> those systems.

Read "confidentiality, integrity, and availability" carefully — that's the actual categorization
question module 2 will ask about the eQMS: what happens if a CAPA record is altered undetected,
exposed to someone who shouldn't see it, or simply unavailable the week an AABB assessor asks for
it. None of that mechanics belongs in this module. What belongs here is noticing that RMF names
that question with more precision, this early in its own process, than either ISO 31000's general
"risk assessment" theme or ICH Q9's "Risk Identification" step does — not because the other two are
worse, but because RMF was built, specifically, around information systems.

## What a reviewer would actually look for

No external body audits Lakeshore against RMF — it isn't a regulation, an AABB Standard, or
anything any outside reviewer checks a private blood establishment's paperwork against. So the
honest version of this section isn't "what would an RMF auditor ask," because no such visitor is
coming. It's: **what would your own CIO, an AABB assessor who stumbles onto the eQMS during a
future reassessment, or you yourself six months from now actually want to find?**

Not three unrelated risk documents in three different drawers, each legible only to the person who
wrote it. What a competent reviewer — internal or external — wants to see is one traceable story
for the eQMS: what was this system's risk judged to be, who decided, what controls got built
because of that judgment, who checked the controls actually work, who accepted what was left over,
and when is that decision getting revisited. That story can legitimately be told in ICH Q9's
vocabulary for the quality-record half of the eQMS and in RMF's vocabulary for the
access-control/availability half — the frameworks don't have to merge into one document. They do
have to both *exist*, in writing, with a name attached to each decision. A bad answer to "show me
the eQMS's risk assessment" sounds exactly like your systems administrator's line from the opening
scenario: "we'll keep an eye on it." A good answer produces a document with a date, a named
decision-maker, and a next review date already on the calendar — regardless of which of the three
vocabularies produced it.

## Common traps

**"Now that Lakeshore uses RMF's structure, RMF is basically a regulatory requirement for the
eQMS."** No. Nothing in federal law requires a private blood establishment to run RMF, issue
anything resembling a federal authorization to operate, or use any of SP 800-37's terms at all.
Lakeshore borrowed the structure because it's a well-built description of a motion worth running
consistently — the identical move this curriculum already showed with AABB accreditation itself,
which `the-aabb-assessment-process` was explicit is voluntary, not a legal requirement to operate.
Calling RMF "required" the moment it's useful is exactly the kind of overstatement that module
warned against.

**"ISO 31000 must be less rigorous than RMF, since it doesn't have a named Authorize step."**
Wrong comparison. ISO 31000 is a general-purpose standard meant to work for a hospital's
enterprise risk register, a manufacturer's supply-chain risk, or a blood center's reputational
risk, equally. It doesn't name one universal sign-off gate because it isn't written around any one
kind of decision the way RMF is written around a federal information system going live. That's a
difference in *scope*, not a difference in how seriously either document takes risk.

**"Since Quality already runs ICH Q9 well, the eQMS doesn't need anything else."** This is the
trap the opening scenario was built to puncture. ICH Q9(R1) is the right tool for the quality-record
risk the eQMS carries — and it should keep doing that job. It was never built to carry the
confidentiality/integrity/availability question RMF's Categorize step asks, or to produce a single
accountable go-live decision the way RMF's Authorize step does. "We already have a risk framework"
and "we have the right risk framework for every question this system raises" are two different
claims.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask which vocabulary produced a given risk decision, and whether that's the right one for the
  question being asked.** ICH Q9 for a quality-record risk, something RMF-shaped for a
  confidentiality/integrity/availability risk — a mismatch between the question and the vocabulary
  answering it is itself a finding.
- **Never let "we're using RMF now" get repeated as "RMF is required."** It isn't, for Lakeshore,
  and letting that drift go uncorrected is exactly the kind of overstatement that costs credibility
  with a CIO or an assessor who knows better.
- **Push for a single, accountable, dated acceptance decision on every system this significant** —
  the thing RMF's Authorize step names explicitly and that your administrator's "I'll keep an eye
  on it" never produced. It doesn't have to use RMF's word for it. It has to exist, in writing,
  with a name on it.
- **When someone cites ISO 31000 or any other paid standard, ask whether they've actually read it
  or are repeating its publicly known themes** — the same discipline this curriculum applies to
  every paywalled source. Describing a standard's shape honestly is fine. Quoting text nobody has
  actually read is not.
- **Expect this to take four more modules, not one meeting.** This module only justifies the
  choice. Categorizing the eQMS, selecting its controls, building and assessing them, making the
  actual authorization call, and tracking what's left on a POA&M (plan of action and milestones)
  are each their own real piece of work — covered next.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator asks, "Now that we're using NIST's framework for the eQMS, are we legally required to get a federal authorization to operate before it goes live?" What do you tell him?

No. An authorization to operate, as NIST SP 800-37 describes it, is a decision made by a senior
federal official for a federal information system — it has no legal application to a private blood
establishment like Lakeshore. Nothing in federal law requires Lakeshore to seek, obtain, or even
name anything called an "authorization to operate" for the eQMS. What Lakeshore *is* doing is
borrowing RMF's structure — including an authorization-style decision point — voluntarily, because
it names a motion worth running consistently, the same way Lakeshore voluntarily holds AABB
accreditation without AABB accreditation being a legal requirement to operate either.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Your Quality Analyst says, "ISO 31000 is basically ICH Q9 with different labels — same number of stages, same process." Is that right?

Not quite, and the imprecision matters. Both describe risk assessment, a response, and ongoing
review — that much genuinely overlaps. But ICH Q9(R1) is a four-stage pharmaceutical/biologics-
specific guideline with a named Risk Acceptance decision inside its Risk Control stage; ISO 31000
is a general-purpose, industry-agnostic standard this curriculum has never independently quoted,
whose publicly known themes (establishing context, risk assessment, risk treatment, monitoring and
review, recording and reporting) don't name one single universal acceptance ceremony the way ICH
Q9 or RMF each do in their own ways. Same underlying motion, genuinely different scope and
precision — not an identical process wearing a different label.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A peer at another blood center tells you they adopted "RMF" but never use the word "Prepare." Did they get it wrong?

Not necessarily — it depends which version of RMF they're describing. Prepare is Revision 2's own
addition to RMF; Revision 1 and earlier public material describe a six-step cycle (Categorize,
Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor) without it. If your peer adopted an older
description of RMF, or simply folds Prepare's activities informally into Categorize without naming
it separately, that's a defensible, if slightly dated, choice — not an error. Worth asking which
revision they actually read, the same instinct this curriculum has taught you to apply to any
citation: the revision number changes what's actually being claimed.
:::

## Where this goes next

The decision is made: the eQMS runs through RMF's structure, end to end, voluntarily, as
Lakeshore's own methodology for this one system. `categorize-and-select-controls` picks up exactly
where Categorize's purpose statement above leaves off — actually asking what happens to Lakeshore
if the eQMS's confidentiality, integrity, or availability fails, and then selecting a set of
controls sized to that answer, not copied wholesale from a template built for a lower-stakes
system.
